meta.topic: 紧致性、度量空间紧性、连通性、可数性公理、吉洪诺夫定理、局部紧与紧化

zh: 设 $X$ 是拓扑空间，$\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ 是 $X$ 的开覆盖：每个 $U_i$ 开且 $X=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$。若对**任意**这样的开覆盖，都存在 $i_1,\dots,i_n\in I$ 使 $X=U_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup U_{i_n}$，则称 $X$ 紧。两个地方不能弱化：必须对一切开覆盖成立；有限个成员必须取自原覆盖。若只要求「存在一个有限开覆盖」，则任何空间都满足（取 $\{X\}$），定义就失去内容。

有限交性质（FIP）：$X$ 紧当且仅当对任意闭集族 $\{F_i\}_{i\in I}$，只要每个有限子族之交非空，就有 $\bigcap_{i\in I}F_i\ne\varnothing$。若全交为空，则 $\{X\setminus F_i\}_{i\in I}$ 是开覆盖；紧性给出有限个成员覆盖 $X$，取补即得对应的有限个 $F_i$ 之交为空，矛盾。反过来，若开覆盖没有有限子覆盖，则其成员的补集组成具有 FIP 的闭集族，而全交为空，与 FIP 矛盾。

设 $K\subset X$ 紧、$F\subset K$ 在 $K$ 中闭（例如 $F$ 在 $X$ 中闭）。给 $F$ 的任一由 $X$ 中开集组成的覆盖 $\{V_j\}_{j\in J}$。因 $K\setminus F$ 在 $K$ 中开，存在 $X$ 中开集 $O$ 使 $K\setminus F=K\cap O$；把 $O$ 添进去，得到 $K$ 的开覆盖。紧性给出有限子覆盖；删去其中可能出现的 $O$，剩下的有限个 $V_j$ 仍覆盖 $F$，故 $F$ 紧。这里用的是 $F$ 在子空间 $K$ 中闭，而不是要求它在 $X$ 中闭。

设 $f:X\to Y$ 连续、$X$ 紧，证明 $f(X)$ 紧。取 $f(X)$ 的任一开覆盖 $\{V_i\}_{i\in I}$（$V_i$ 在 $Y$ 中开），则 $\{f^{-1}(V_i)\}_{i\in I}$ 是 $X$ 的开覆盖；紧性给出有限个 $f^{-1}(V_{i_1}),\dots,f^{-1}(V_{i_n})$ 覆盖 $X$，于是 $f(X)\subset V_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{i_n}$。故 $f(X)$ 紧。若 $X\ne\varnothing$，取 $Y=\mathbb R$ 即得最值定理：$f(X)$ 是 $\mathbb R$ 的紧子集，因而有界且闭，$\sup f(X)$ 与 $\inf f(X)$ 都属于 $f(X)$。

紧 Hausdorff 空间正规。先证正则性：设 $B\subset X$ 闭、$x
otin B$。因 $X$ 紧、$B$ 闭，$B$ 紧；对每个 $y\in B$ 取不交开集 $U_y
i x$、$V_y
i y$，有限个 $V_{y_1},\dots,V_{y_n}$ 覆盖 $B$。令 $U= igcap_k U_{y_k}$、$V= igcup_k V_{y_k}$，则 $U,V$ 不交开集，$x\in U$、$B\subset V$。再设 $A,B$ 为不交闭集；对每个 $a\in A$ 用正则性取不交开集 $U_a
i a$、$W_a\supset B$。$A$ 紧（紧空间的闭子集），有限个 $U_{a_k}$ 覆盖 $A$；令 $U= igcup_k U_{a_k}$、$W= igcap_k W_{a_k}$，则 $U,W$ 不交开集分离 $A,B$。故 $X$ 正规（$T_4$）。
en: Let $X$ be a topological space and let $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover: each $U_i$ is open and $X=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$. We call $X$ compact if **every** such cover contains finitely many members that still cover $X$, i.e. $X=U_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup U_{i_n}$ for some $i_1,\dots,i_n\in I$. Two aspects must not be weakened: the condition is imposed on all open covers, and the finitely many members must come from the given cover. Requiring merely that 「a finite open cover exists」 is vacuous, since $\{X\}$ always is one.

Finite intersection property (FIP): $X$ is compact iff for every family of closed sets $\{F_i\}_{i\in I}$, the nonemptiness of every finite subintersection implies $\bigcap_{i\in I}F_i\ne\varnothing$. If the total intersection is empty, then $\{X\setminus F_i\}_{i\in I}$ is an open cover; compactness gives finitely many members covering $X$, and taking complements gives a finite subfamily of $F_i$ with empty intersection, a contradiction. Conversely, if an open cover has no finite subcover, the complements of its members form a family of closed sets with the FIP but empty total intersection.

Let $K\subset X$ be compact and $F\subset K$ closed in $K$ (for instance, closed in $X$). Given any cover $\{V_j\}_{j\in J}$ of $F$ by open sets of $X$. Since $K\setminus F$ is open in $K$, there is an open $O\subset X$ with $K\setminus F=K\cap O$; adjoining $O$ gives an open cover of $K$. Compactness yields a finite subcover; discarding $O$ if it occurs, the remaining finitely many $V_j$ still cover $F$, so $F$ is compact. The hypothesis used is closedness in the subspace $K$, not in $X$.

Let $X$ be Hausdorff and $K\subset X$ compact; we show $K$ is closed. Take $x
otin K$. For each $y\in K$, Hausdorffness gives disjoint open sets $U_y
i x$ and $V_y
i y$. The family $\{V_y\}_{y\in K}$ covers $K$, so finitely many $V_{y_1},\dots,V_{y_n}$ cover $K$. Put $U=U_{y_1}\cap\cdots\cap U_{y_n}$; then $U$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$ with $U\cap K=\varnothing$, hence $X\setminus K$ is open and $K$ is closed. Hausdorffness cannot be dropped: the cofinite topology on an infinite set is $T_1$, and every infinite proper subset is compact but not closed.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and $X$ compact; we show $f(X)$ is compact. Take any open cover $\{V_i\}_{i\in I}$ of $f(X)$ by open sets of $Y$. Then $\{f^{-1}(V_i)\}_{i\in I}$ is an open cover of $X$; compactness gives finitely many $f^{-1}(V_{i_1}),\dots,f^{-1}(V_{i_n})$ covering $X$, hence $f(X)\subset V_{i_1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{i_n}$. Thus $f(X)$ is compact. If $X\ne\varnothing$, taking $Y=\mathbb R$ gives the extreme value theorem: $f(X)$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb R$, hence bounded and closed, and $\sup f(X)$, $\inf f(X)$ both belong to $f(X)$.

A compact Hausdorff space is normal. First prove regularity: let $B\subset X$ be closed and $x
otin B$. Since $X$ is compact and $B$ closed, $B$ is compact; for each $y\in B$ choose disjoint open sets $U_y
i x$ and $V_y
i y$, and finitely many $V_{y_1},\dots,V_{y_n}$ cover $B$. Set $U= igcap_k U_{y_k}$ and $V= igcup_k V_{y_k}$; then $U,V$ are disjoint open sets with $x\in U$ and $B\subset V$. Now let $A,B$ be disjoint closed sets. For each $a\in A$, regularity gives disjoint open sets $U_a
i a$ and $W_a\supset B$. The set $A$ is compact (closed in a compact space), so finitely many $U_{a_k}$ cover $A$; setting $U= igcup_k U_{a_k}$ and $W= igcap_k W_{a_k}$ gives disjoint open sets separating $A$ and $B$. Hence $X$ is normal ($T_4$).

zh: 设 $(X,d)$ 是度量空间。列紧指每个序列都有收敛于 $X$ 中点的子序列；全有界（完全有界）指对每个 $\varepsilon>0$ 存在有限个 $x_1,\dots,x_n$ 使 $X=\bigcup_{k=1}^n B(x_k,\varepsilon)$（有限 $\varepsilon$-网）；完备指每个 Cauchy 序列收敛。基本定理是 $$\begin{aligned}&\text{紧}\iff\text{列紧}\\ &\iff\text{完备且全有界},\end{aligned}$$ 三者只在度量空间语境下等价；一般拓扑空间中紧与列紧可以不同。

紧 $\Rightarrow$ 全有界。固定 $\varepsilon>0$，族 $\{B(x,\varepsilon):x\in X\}$ 显然覆盖 $X$；由紧性取有限子覆盖 $B(x_1,\varepsilon),\dots,B(x_n,\varepsilon)$，这正是有限 $\varepsilon$-网。这里用的是「任意开覆盖」，而不是「存在有限覆盖」；有界性只给出一个大球，不能推出对每个 $\varepsilon$ 的有限网。

紧 $\Rightarrow$ 列紧，从而完备。任取序列 $(x_n)$。若某个值出现无限多次，取常值子序列即收敛。否则 $\{x_n\}$ 无限；若它没有聚点，则每点 $x$ 有开邻域 $U_x$ 只含有限多个 $x_n$，$\{U_x\}$ 的开覆盖由紧性有有限子覆盖，于是总共只含有限多个 $x_n$，与无限多互异项矛盾。故有聚点 $p$，取 $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ 使 $d(x_{n_k},p)<1/k$，得收敛子序列。再若 $(x_n)$ 是 Cauchy 序列，其收敛子列极限为 $p$，由三角不等式 $d(x_n,p)\le d(x_n,x_{n_k})+d(x_{n_k},p)\to0$，故 $x_n\to p$，空间完备。

全有界 $\Rightarrow$ 每个序列有 Cauchy 子序列；再加完备即得列紧。对每个 $k$ 取有限 $1/k$-网。从原序列中取一个落在某个 $1$-网球中的无限子序列，再从中取落在某个 $1/2$-网球中的无限子序列，如此逐层抽取；第 $k$ 层子序列的项两两距离 $<2/k$。用对角线取 $n_1<n_2<\cdots$，使 $x_{n_k}$ 属于第 $k$ 层子序列；则对 $j,l\ge k$，$d(x_{n_j},x_{n_l})<2/k$，故 $(x_{n_k})$ 是 Cauchy 序列。完备性使它收敛，于是「完备 + 全有界 $\Rightarrow$ 列紧」。

列紧 $\Rightarrow$ 紧。先由列紧推出全有界：若存在 $\varepsilon>0$ 没有有限 $\varepsilon$-网，则递归选 $x_n$ 使 $d(x_n,x_m)\ge\varepsilon$（$m<n$），这样的序列没有 Cauchy 子序列，矛盾。再证覆盖 $\{U_i\}$ 有 Lebesgue 数：若没有，则对每个 $n$ 存在 $x_n$ 使 $B(x_n,1/n)$ 不包含于任何 $U_i$；列紧给出子列 $x_{n_k}\to x\in U_j$，取 $r>0$ 使 $B(x,r)\subset U_j$，当 $k$ 大时 $d(x_{n_k},x)<r/2$ 且 $1/n_k<r/2$，于是 $B(x_{n_k},1/n_k)\subset B(x,r)\subset U_j$，矛盾。故存在 $\delta>0$，凡直径 $<\delta$ 的集合都落在某个 $U_i$ 中。取有限 $\delta/3$-网 $y_1,\dots,y_m$，每个 $B(y_k,\delta/3)$ 的直径 $<2\delta/3<\delta$，故含于某个 $U_{i_k}$；这 $m$ 个 $U_{i_k}$ 覆盖 $X$，即得有限子覆盖。

Heine–Borel 与无穷维反例。若 $K\subset\mathbb R^n$ 紧，则由紧集在 Hausdorff 空间中闭得 $K$ 闭；用覆盖 $\{B(0,m)\}_{m\ge1}$ 得 $K$ 有界。反之若 $K$ 有界闭，则 $K\subset[-M,M]^n$；$[-M,M]^n$ 完备且全有界（按坐标取有限网格），故紧，其闭子集 $K$ 也紧。因此 $$\begin{aligned}&K\subset\mathbb R^n\ \text{紧}\\ &\iff K\ \text{有界且闭}.\end{aligned}$$ 这只对有限维成立：$\ell^2$ 的闭单位球有界、闭、完备，但标准基 $e_n$ 满足 $\|e_n-e_m\|=\sqrt2$，有限个半径 $1/2$ 的球盖不住它，故不全有界、不紧。
en: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space. Sequential compactness means every sequence has a subsequence converging to a point of $X$; total boundedness means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there are finitely many $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with $X=\bigcup_{k=1}^n B(x_k,\varepsilon)$ (a finite $\varepsilon$-net); completeness means every Cauchy sequence converges. The basic theorem is $$\begin{aligned}&\text{compact}\iff\text{sequentially compact}\\ &\iff\text{complete and totally bounded},\end{aligned}$$ an equivalence that holds only in the metric setting; in general topological spaces compactness and sequential compactness can differ.

Compactness implies total boundedness. Fix $\varepsilon>0$; the family $\{B(x,\varepsilon):x\in X\}$ plainly covers $X$, so compactness gives a finite subcover $B(x_1,\varepsilon),\dots,B(x_n,\varepsilon)$, which is a finite $\varepsilon$-net. This uses the condition on **every** open cover, not the existence of some finite cover; boundedness gives only one large ball and does not produce finite $\varepsilon$-nets for all $\varepsilon$.

Compactness implies sequential compactness, hence completeness. Take a sequence $(x_n)$. If some value occurs infinitely often, a constant subsequence converges. Otherwise $\{x_n\}$ is infinite; if it had no cluster point, every $x$ would have an open neighbourhood $U_x$ containing only finitely many $x_n$, and the open cover $\{U_x\}$ would have a finite subcover by compactness, so only finitely many $x_n$ would occur, contradicting the infinitely many distinct terms. Hence there is a cluster point $p$, and choosing $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ with $d(x_{n_k},p)<1/k$ gives a convergent subsequence. If $(x_n)$ is Cauchy, its convergent subsequence has limit $p$, and $d(x_n,p)\le d(x_n,x_{n_k})+d(x_{n_k},p)\to0$, so $x_n\to p$; thus $X$ is complete.

Total boundedness implies that every sequence has a Cauchy subsequence; together with completeness this gives sequential compactness. For each $k$ take a finite $1/k$-net. Pass to an infinite subsequence lying in one ball of the $1$-net, then to an infinite subsequence of that lying in one ball of the $1/2$-net, and so on; terms in the $k$-th subsequence are pairwise at distance $<2/k$. Choose $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ diagonally so that $x_{n_k}$ belongs to the $k$-th subsequence; then for $j,l\ge k$, $d(x_{n_j},x_{n_l})<2/k$, so $(x_{n_k})$ is Cauchy. Completeness makes it converge, hence 「complete + totally bounded implies sequentially compact」.

Sequential compactness implies compactness. First, sequential compactness implies total boundedness: if some $\varepsilon>0$ admitted no finite $\varepsilon$-net, one could recursively choose $x_n$ with $d(x_n,x_m)\ge\varepsilon$ for $m<n$, and such a sequence has no Cauchy subsequence, a contradiction. Next, an open cover $\{U_i\}$ has a Lebesgue number: otherwise, for each $n$ there is $x_n$ with $B(x_n,1/n)$ contained in no $U_i$; sequential compactness gives a subsequence $x_{n_k}\to x\in U_j$, and choosing $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subset U_j$, for large $k$ we have $d(x_{n_k},x)<r/2$ and $1/n_k<r/2$, so $B(x_{n_k},1/n_k)\subset B(x,r)\subset U_j$, a contradiction. Thus there is $\delta>0$ such that every set of diameter $<\delta$ lies in some $U_i$. Take a finite $\delta/3$-net $y_1,\dots,y_m$; each $B(y_k,\delta/3)$ has diameter $<2\delta/3<\delta$, hence lies in some $U_{i_k}$, and these $m$ sets $U_{i_k}$ cover $X$, giving a finite subcover.

Heine–Borel and an infinite-dimensional counterexample. If $K\subset\mathbb R^n$ is compact, then $K$ is closed because compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed, and bounded by applying compactness to the cover $\{B(0,m)\}_{m\ge1}$. Conversely, if $K$ is bounded and closed, then $K\subset[-M,M]^n$; the cube $[-M,M]^n$ is complete and totally bounded (use a finite grid in each coordinate), hence compact, and so is its closed subset $K$. Therefore $$\begin{aligned}&K\subset\mathbb R^n\ \text{is compact}\\ &\iff K\ \text{is bounded and closed}.\end{aligned}$$ This holds only in finite dimensions: the closed unit ball of $\ell^2$ is bounded, closed and complete, but its standard basis vectors satisfy $\|e_n-e_m\|=\sqrt2$, so finitely many balls of radius $1/2$ cannot cover it; it is not totally bounded and not compact.

zh: 称 $X$ 连通，若不存在非空不交开集 $U,V$ 使 $X=U\cup V$；这样的一对 $U,V$ 称为 $X$ 的分离。因 $V=X\setminus U$，等价地，$X$ 中除 $\varnothing$ 与 $X$ 外没有既开又闭的子集；把「开」换成「闭」也得到同一概念。子集 $A\subset X$ 连通指 $A$ 配子空间拓扑连通；等价地，$A$ 不连通当且仅当存在 $X$ 中开集 $U,V$ 使 $A\subset U\cup V$、$A\cap U\ne\varnothing$、$A\cap V\ne\varnothing$ 且 $A\cap U\cap V=\varnothing$。

连续像保持连通。设 $f:X\to Y$ 连续、$X$ 连通。若 $f(X)\subset U\cup V$，其中 $U,V$ 是 $Y$ 中开集，$f(X)\cap U$ 与 $f(X)\cap V$ 非空，且 $f(X)\cap U\cap V=\varnothing$，则 $f^{-1}(U)$ 与 $f^{-1}(V)$ 是 $X$ 的非空不交开集，且并为 $X$，与 $X$ 连通矛盾。故 $f(X)$ 连通。取 $X=[a,b]$、$Y=\mathbb R$：连续像 $f([a,b])$ 是 $\mathbb R$ 的连通子集，即是区间，于是 $f(a)<c<f(b)$ 时必有 $c\in f([a,b])$，这就是介值定理。

闭包保持连通。设 $A$ 连通，若 $\overline A$ 有分离 $\overline A=U\cup V$（$U,V$ 在 $\overline A$ 中相对开、不交非空），则 $A=(A\cap U)\cup(A\cap V)$。若 $A\cap U$ 与 $A\cap V$ 都非空，就得到 $A$ 的分离，矛盾；故不妨 $A\cap U=\varnothing$，即 $A\subset V$。$V$ 在 $\overline A$ 中相对闭，于是 $\overline A\subset V$，与 $U\ne\varnothing$ 矛盾。故 $\overline A$ 连通。其次，若 $A,B$ 连通且 $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$，而 $A\cup B=U\cup V$ 是分离，则 $A$ 连通使 $A$ 落在 $U$ 或 $V$ 中，$B$ 也如此；公共点迫使 $A,B$ 落在同一块，另一块为空，矛盾。故 $A\cup B$ 连通。
道路连通 $\Rightarrow$ 连通。固定 $x_0\in X$。考虑所有从 $x_0$ 出发的道路 $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$；每个像 $\gamma([0,1])$ 都是含 $x_0$ 的连通集。路径连通保证这些像的并等于 $X$（每个 $x$ 都在某条这样的道路的终点），由第 3 步，这个并连通。反向不成立；下一步的拓扑学家的正弦曲线就是连通而不道路连通的例子。

拓扑学家的正弦曲线 $S=\Gamma\cup(\{0\}\times[-1,1])$，其中 $\Gamma=\{(x,\sin(1/x)):0<x\le1\}$。$\Gamma$ 是连续映射 $x\mapsto(x,\sin(1/x))$ 在连通集 $(0,1]$ 上的像，故连通。又 $S=\overline\Gamma$：对每个 $y\in[-1,1]$，取 $x_k\to0^+$ 使 $\sin(1/x_k)=y$（例如 $1/x_k=\arcsin y+2k\pi$），则 $(0,y)$ 是 $\Gamma$ 的极限点；而 $\Gamma$ 的极限点都落在 $S$ 中。由第 3 步，闭包 $\overline\Gamma=S$ 连通。

但 $S$ 不道路连通。反设道路 $p:[0,1]\to S$ 满足 $p(0)=(0,y_0)$、$p(1)\in\Gamma$。令 $t_0=\sup\{t\in[0,1]:x(p(t))=0\}$；由 $x(p(t))$ 连续，$x(p(t_0))=0$，且 $t_0<1$；又当 $t>t_0$ 时必有 $x(p(t))>0$，故 $p(t)\in\Gamma$，即 $y(p(t))=\sin(1/x(p(t)))$。当 $t\to t_0^+$ 时 $x(p(t))\to0^+$。对任意 $\eta>0$，先取 $t_1\in(t_0,t_0+\eta)$ 使 $s_1=x(p(t_1))$ 充分小；在 $[t_0,t_1]$ 上用介值定理，$x(p(t))$ 取遍 $(0,s_1)$ 中的值，特别可取到 $1/(\pi/2+2k\pi)$ 与 $1/(3\pi/2+2k\pi)$，对应 $y(p(t))$ 为 $1$ 与 $-1$。于是 $t\to t_0^+$ 时 $y(p(t))$ 在 $1$ 与 $-1$ 之间振荡；连续性要求存在 $\delta>0$ 使 $t\in(t_0,t_0+\delta)$ 时 $|y(p(t))-y_0|<1/2$，但该区间内既有 $y=1$ 又有 $y=-1$，而 $1$ 与 $-1$ 中至少有一个与 $y_0$ 的距离不小于 $1$，不可能满足此不等式，矛盾。故 $S$ 连通但不道路连通。

连通分支：在 $X$ 上定义 $x\sim y$ 当且仅当存在连通集同时含 $x,y$；这是等价关系（传递性由第 3 步保证：若连通集 $A$ 含 $x,y$，连通集 $B$ 含 $y,z$，则 $A\cup B$ 连通且含 $x,z$）。固定 $x$，所有含 $x$ 的连通集之并含公共点 $x$，由第 3 步连通，且它就是 $x$ 的等价类；故每个等价类连通且极大，称为连通分支，各分支两两不交且并为 $X$。每个分支 $C$ 闭：由第 3 步 $\overline C$ 连通且包含 $C$，极大性给出 $\overline C=C$。道路连通分支用「存在连接两点的道路」定义，因道路的像连通，每个道路分支含于某个连通分支，故道路分支的划分更细；$S$ 只有一个连通分支（自身），却有两个道路分支（竖直线段与 $\Gamma$）。当 $X$ 局部道路连通时，每个连通分支既开又闭，且连通 $\iff$ 道路连通。
en: $X$ is connected if there are no nonempty disjoint open sets $U,V$ with $X=U\cup V$; such a pair is called a separation of $X$. Since then $V=X\setminus U$, equivalently no subset of $X$ other than $\varnothing$ and $X$ is both open and closed; replacing 「open」 by 「closed」 gives the same notion. A subset $A\subset X$ is connected when $A$ with the subspace topology is connected; equivalently, $A$ is disconnected iff there are open sets $U,V$ of $X$ with $A\subset U\cup V$, $A\cap U\ne\varnothing$, $A\cap V\ne\varnothing$ and $A\cap U\cap V=\varnothing$.

Continuous images preserve connectedness. Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and $X$ connected. If $f(X)\subset U\cup V$, where $U,V$ are open in $Y$, $f(X)\cap U$ and $f(X)\cap V$ are nonempty, and $f(X)\cap U\cap V=\varnothing$, then $f^{-1}(U)$ and $f^{-1}(V)$ are nonempty disjoint open sets whose union is $X$, contradicting connectedness. Hence $f(X)$ is connected. Taking $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=\mathbb R$: the continuous image $f([a,b])$ is a connected subset of $\mathbb R$, hence an interval, so $f(a)<c<f(b)$ implies $c\in f([a,b])$ — the intermediate value theorem.

Closures preserve connectedness. Let $A$ be connected and suppose $\overline A=U\cup V$ is a separation, with $U,V$ relatively open in $\overline A$, disjoint and nonempty. Then $A=(A\cap U)\cup(A\cap V)$; if both intersections were nonempty we would have a separation of $A$, so assume $A\cap U=\varnothing$, i.e. $A\subset V$. Since $V$ is relatively closed in $\overline A$, it follows that $\overline A\subset V$, contradicting $U\ne\varnothing$. Hence $\overline A$ is connected. Also, if $A,B$ are connected and $A\cap B\ne\varnothing$, and $A\cup B=U\cup V$ is a separation, then connectedness puts $A$ wholly in $U$ or in $V$, and likewise $B$; the common point forces both in the same piece, leaving the other empty, a contradiction. Thus $A\cup B$ is connected.

Path connectedness implies connectedness. Fix $x_0\in X$. Consider all paths $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$ starting at $x_0$; each image $\gamma([0,1])$ is a connected set containing $x_0$. Path connectedness ensures that the union of these images is $X$ (every $x$ is the endpoint of such a path), so by Step 3 the union is connected. The converse fails; the topologist's sine curve in the next step is connected but not path connected.

The topologist's sine curve is $S=\Gamma\cup(\{0\}\times[-1,1])$, where $\Gamma=\{(x,\sin(1/x)):0<x\le1\}$. $\Gamma$ is the image of the connected set $(0,1]$ under the continuous map $x\mapsto(x,\sin(1/x))$, hence connected. Moreover $S=\overline\Gamma$: for each $y\in[-1,1]$, choose $x_k\to0^+$ with $\sin(1/x_k)=y$ (for instance $1/x_k=\arcsin y+2k\pi$), so $(0,y)$ is a limit point of $\Gamma$; and every limit point of $\Gamma$ lies in $S$. By Step 3, the closure $\overline\Gamma=S$ is connected.

However, $S$ is not path connected. Suppose a path $p:[0,1]\to S$ satisfies $p(0)=(0,y_0)$ and $p(1)\in\Gamma$. Let $t_0=\sup\{t\in[0,1]:x(p(t))=0\}$. By continuity of $x(p(t))$, $x(p(t_0))=0$, and $t_0<1$; also $x(p(t))>0$ for $t>t_0$, so $p(t)\in\Gamma$ and $y(p(t))=\sin(1/x(p(t)))$. As $t\to t_0^+$, $x(p(t))\to0^+$. Given any $\eta>0$, choose $t_1\in(t_0,t_0+\eta)$ with $s_1=x(p(t_1))$ small; by the intermediate value theorem applied to $x(p(t))$ on $[t_0,t_1]$, it assumes every value in $(0,s_1)$, in particular $1/(\pi/2+2k\pi)$ and $1/(3\pi/2+2k\pi)$ for large $k$, where $y(p(t))$ equals $1$ and $-1$ respectively. Thus $y(p(t))$ oscillates between $1$ and $-1$ arbitrarily close to $t_0$, so it cannot converge to $y(p(t_0))=y_0$; continuity requires $|y(p(t))-y_0|<1/2$ on some interval $(t_0,t_0+\delta)$, but at least one of $1$ and $-1$ is at distance at least $1$ from $y_0$, so it cannot satisfy this inequality. Hence $S$ is connected but not path connected.

Components: define $x\sim y$ iff some connected set contains both. This is an equivalence relation (transitivity follows from Step 3: if a connected set $A$ contains $x,y$ and a connected set $B$ contains $y,z$, then $A\cup B$ is connected and contains $x,z$). For fixed $x$, the union of all connected sets containing $x$ has the common point $x$, hence is connected by Step 3, and it is exactly the equivalence class of $x$; thus each class is connected and maximal, is called a connected component, and the components are pairwise disjoint and cover $X$. Each component $C$ is closed: by Step 3, $\overline C$ is connected and contains $C$, so maximality gives $\overline C=C$. Path components are defined by 「joined by a path」; since the image of a path is connected, every path component lies in a connected component, so the path partition is finer. The curve $S$ has one connected component (itself) but two path components (the vertical segment and $\Gamma$). When $X$ is locally path connected, every component is both open and closed, and connectedness is equivalent to path connectedness.

zh: 四个「小性」定义。第一可数 $C_1$：每点 $x$ 有可数邻域基 $\{B_n(x)\}$，即每个含 $x$ 的开集 $U$ 都含某个 $B_n(x)$。第二可数 $C_2$：拓扑有可数基 $\mathcal B=\{B_n\}$。可分：存在可数稠密子集 $D$，$\overline D=X$。Lindelöf：每个开覆盖有可数子覆盖。度量空间自动 $C_1$（取 $B(x,1/n)$），但 $C_1$ 不蕴含 $C_2$：$C_1$ 是逐点的可数信息，$C_2$ 是整个拓扑的可数信息。

$C_2\Rightarrow C_1$ 且 $C_2\Rightarrow$ 可分。若 $\mathcal B$ 是可数基，固定 $x$，则 $\mathcal B_x=\{B\in\mathcal B:x\in B\}$ 可数；对任意开集 $U
i x$，取 $B\in\mathcal B$ 使 $x\in B\subset U$，故 $\mathcal B_x$ 是 $x$ 的可数邻域基。再从每个非空 $B\in\mathcal B$ 中取一点组成 $D$，$D$ 可数；任取非空开集 $U$，它有基元素 $B\subset U$，而 $D\cap B
e\varnothing$，故 $D\cap U
e\varnothing$，$\overline D=X$。

$C_2\Rightarrow$ Lindelöf。设 $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ 是开覆盖。令 $\mathcal B'=\{B\in\mathcal B:B\subset U_i\ \text{对某个}\ i\}$；每个 $x$ 属于某个 $U_i$，而 $\mathcal B$ 是基，故有 $B\in\mathcal B$ 使 $x\in B\subset U_i$，所以 $\mathcal B'$ 覆盖 $X$。$\mathcal B'$ 可数；对每个 $B\in\mathcal B'$ 选一个包含它的 $U_{i(B)}$，这些 $U_{i(B)}$ 是可数子覆盖。

反向蕴含一般不成立。Sorgenfrey 直线 $(\mathbb R,\mathcal T_{\text{下限}})$ 以 $[a,b)$ 为基：$\mathbb Q$ 与每个 $[a,b)$ 相交，故可分；但它没有可数基——对每个 $x$，$[x,x+1)$ 开，取基元素 $B_x$ 使 $x\in B_x\subset[x,x+1)$，则 $x=\min B_x$（$B_x$ 是若干 $[a,b)$ 之并，含 $x$ 的那个必须从 $x$ 开始），于是 $x\mapsto B_x$ 单射，不可数多个互异基元素，矛盾。另有：Sorgenfrey 直线本身 Lindelöf 但不 $C_2$；Sorgenfrey 平面可分但不 Lindelöf；不可数离散空间 $C_1$ 但既不 $C_2$ 也不 Lindelöf。故从 $C_2$ 出发的三条箭头都不能反转。

度量空间中三者等价。设 $(X,d)$ 可分，取可数稠密集 $D$，令 $\mathcal B=\{B(d,1/n):d\in D,n\ge1\}$，可数。任取开集 $U$ 与 $x\in U$，取 $r>0$ 使 $B(x,r)\subset U$；取 $n$ 使 $1/n<r/2$，由稠密性取 $d\in D\cap B(x,1/n)$。则 $x\in B(d,1/n)\subset B(x,2/n)\subset B(x,r)\subset U$，故 $\mathcal B$ 是基，$X$ 是 $C_2$。结合第 2、3 步得 $$\text{可分}\Rightarrow C_2\Rightarrow\text{Lindelöf}.$$ 反向 Lindelöf $\Rightarrow$ 可分：对每个 $n$，覆盖 $\{B(x,1/n):x\in X\}$ 有可数子覆盖，其球心组成可数 $1/n$-网，全部球心合起来可数稠密。故度量空间中可分 $\iff C_2\iff$ Lindelöf。

推论与边界。紧度量空间必可分、必 $C_2$：对每个 $n$，覆盖 $\{B(x,1/n)\}$ 有有限子覆盖，网心全体是可数稠密集，再由第 5 步得 $C_2$。$C_1,C_2$ 对子空间遗传、对可数积保持；可分性不遗传（Sorgenfrey 平面的反对角线是不可数离散子空间），$C_2$ 也不被不可数积保持。紧 Hausdorff 不必 $C_2$（如 $[0,1]^I$，$I$ 不可数，不是第一可数）；反过来，Urysohn 度量化定理说「正则（含 $T_1$）+ $C_2$ $\Rightarrow$ 可度量化」，说明 $C_2$ 是把拓扑空间纳入度量框架的关键可数性条件。
en: Four smallness properties. First countable ($C_1$): every point $x$ has a countable neighbourhood base $\{B_n(x)\}$, i.e. every open $U\ni x$ contains some $B_n(x)$. Second countable ($C_2$): the topology has a countable base $\mathcal B=\{B_n\}$. Separable: there is a countable dense subset $D$, $\overline D=X$. Lindelöf: every open cover has a countable subcover. Every metric space is $C_1$ (take $B(x,1/n)$), but $C_1$ does not imply $C_2$: $C_1$ is countable information at each point, while $C_2$ is countable information for the whole topology.

$C_2\Rightarrow C_1$ and $C_2\Rightarrow$ separable. If $\mathcal B$ is a countable base and $x$ is fixed, then $\mathcal B_x=\{B\in\mathcal B:x\in B\}$ is countable; for every open $U
i x$ there is $B\in\mathcal B$ with $x\in B\subset U$, so $\mathcal B_x$ is a countable neighbourhood base at $x$. Next choose one point from each nonempty $B\in\mathcal B$ to form $D$, which is countable; every nonempty open $U$ contains some base element $B\subset U$, and $D\cap B
e\varnothing$, so $D\cap U
e\varnothing$ and $\overline D=X$.

$C_2\Rightarrow$ Lindelöf. Let $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ be an open cover and let $\mathcal B'=\{B\in\mathcal B:B\subset U_i\ \text{for some}\ i\}$. Every $x$ lies in some $U_i$, and since $\mathcal B$ is a base there is $B\in\mathcal B$ with $x\in B\subset U_i$; hence $\mathcal B'$ covers $X$. The family $\mathcal B'$ is countable; for each $B\in\mathcal B'$ choose one $U_{i(B)}$ containing it. These $U_{i(B)}$ form a countable subcover.

The converses fail in general. The Sorgenfrey line $(\mathbb R,\mathcal T_{\text{lower limit}})$ has a base of half-open intervals $[a,b)$: $\mathbb Q$ meets every $[a,b)$, so the space is separable; but it has no countable base. Indeed, for each $x$, the set $[x,x+1)$ is open, so a base element $B_x$ would satisfy $x\in B_x\subset[x,x+1)$. Since $B_x$ is a union of intervals $[a,b)$, the member containing $x$ must start at $x$, hence $x=\min B_x$; thus $x\mapsto B_x$ is injective, producing uncountably many distinct base elements, a contradiction. Moreover, the Sorgenfrey line itself is Lindelöf but not $C_2$; the Sorgenfrey plane is separable but not Lindelöf; and an uncountable discrete space is $C_1$ but neither $C_2$ nor Lindelöf. Hence none of the three arrows from $C_2$ reverses.

In metric spaces the three notions coincide. Let $(X,d)$ be separable with countable dense $D$, and let $\mathcal B=\{B(d,1/n):d\in D,\ n\ge1\}$, which is countable. Given open $U$ and $x\in U$, choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subset U$; choose $n$ with $1/n<r/2$, and use density to pick $d\in D\cap B(x,1/n)$. Then $x\in B(d,1/n)\subset B(x,2/n)\subset B(x,r)\subset U$, so $\mathcal B$ is a base and $X$ is $C_2$. With Steps 2 and 3, $$\text{separable}\Rightarrow C_2\Rightarrow\text{Lindelöf}.$$ Conversely, Lindelöf implies separable: for each $n$, the cover $\{B(x,1/n):x\in X\}$ has a countable subcover, whose centres form a countable $1/n$-net; the union of all these centres is a countable dense set. Thus in a metric space, separable $\iff C_2\iff$ Lindelöf.

Consequences and limits. A compact metric space is separable and $C_2$: for each $n$ the cover $\{B(x,1/n)\}$ has a finite subcover, the union of all these finite nets is a countable dense set, and Step 5 gives $C_2$. The properties $C_1$ and $C_2$ are hereditary and preserved by countable products; separability is not hereditary (the anti-diagonal of the Sorgenfrey plane is an uncountable discrete subspace), and $C_2$ is not preserved by uncountable products. A compact Hausdorff space need not be $C_2$: $[0,1]^I$ with uncountable $I$ is compact Hausdorff but not first countable. Conversely, the Urysohn metrisation theorem says that a regular $T_1$ space with a countable base is metrisable, which is why $C_2$ is the key countability condition for metrisation.

zh: 吉洪诺夫定理：若 $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ 是一族紧空间，则积空间 $X=\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ 在**积拓扑**下紧，指标集 $I$ 任意。积拓扑由投影 $\pi_i:X\to X_i$ 的原像 $\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)$ 生成的子基给出，等价地，其基元素 $\prod_i U_i$ 中除有限多个 $i$ 外 $U_i=X_i$。必须强调「积拓扑」：若改用箱拓扑（允许无限多个坐标取真开子集），结论不成立。

有限积用管引理。设 $X,Y$ 紧，$W\subset X\times Y$ 开且包含整条横梁 $\{x_0\}\times Y$。对每个 $y\in Y$ 取基本开集 $U_y\times V_y\subset W$ 含 $(x_0,y)$；$\{V_y\}$ 覆盖紧空间 $Y$，取有限子覆盖 $V_{y_1},\dots,V_{y_n}$。令 $U=U_{y_1}\cap\cdots\cap U_{y_n}$，则 $U\ni x_0$ 开且 $U\times Y\subset\bigcup_k U_{y_k}\times V_{y_k}\subset W$，这就是管引理。更一般地，若一族开集 $\{W_j\}$ 覆盖横梁 $\{x_0\}\times Y$，对每个 $y$ 取包含 $(x_0,y)$ 的 $W_{j(y)}$ 与基本开集 $U_y\times V_y\subset W_{j(y)}$，同样的有限子覆盖论证给出 $x_0$ 的开邻域 $U$ 使 $U\times Y$ 被有限个 $W_j$ 覆盖。

用管引理证 $X\times Y$ 紧。设 $\{W_j\}$ 是 $X\times Y$ 的开覆盖。固定 $x\in X$，横梁 $\{x\}\times Y$ 被覆盖；由第 2 步，存在开邻域 $U\ni x$ 使 $U\times Y$ 被有限个 $W_j$ 覆盖。把所有具有这一性质的开集 $U$ 收集成族 $\mathcal U$，它覆盖紧空间 $X$，故有有限个 $U_{x_1},\dots,U_{x_m}\in\mathcal U$ 覆盖 $X$；每个 $U_{x_k}\times Y$ 由有限个 $W_j$ 覆盖，把这 $m$ 组有限个 $W_j$ 合并，得到原覆盖的有限子覆盖。故 $X\times Y$ 紧。归纳得任意有限积紧；全程只作有限次选取，不需要选择公理。

无限积需要亚历山大子基定理：若拓扑空间有一组子基 $\mathcal S$，使每个由 $\mathcal S$ 中元素组成的开覆盖都有有限子覆盖，则空间紧。证明要点：若存在无有限子覆盖的开覆盖，用 Zorn 引理取一个极大的无有限子覆盖开覆盖 $\mathcal U$。极大性推出 $\mathcal U$ 对有限交封闭：若 $U,V\in\mathcal U$ 而 $U\cap V\notin\mathcal U$，则 $\mathcal U\cup\{U\cap V\}$ 有有限子覆盖，因 $U\cap V\subset U$，把它换成 $U$ 就得到 $\mathcal U$ 的有限子覆盖，矛盾。对每点 $x$，取 $U_x\in\mathcal U$ 与子基元素 $S_{x,1},\dots,S_{x,m}$ 使 $x\in\bigcap_j S_{x,j}\subset U_x$。若所有 $S_{x,j}\notin\mathcal U$，极大性给出 $X=S_{x,j}\cup A_j$，其中 $A_j$ 是有限个 $\mathcal U$ 成员之并；于是 $$\begin{aligned}X&=\Big(\bigcap_j S_{x,j}\Big)\cup\bigcup_j A_j\\ &\subset U_x\cup\bigcup_j A_j,\end{aligned}$$ 右端是 $\mathcal U$ 的有限子覆盖，矛盾。故 $\mathcal U$ 中的子基元素全体覆盖 $X$；按假设取有限子覆盖，仍是 $\mathcal U$ 的有限子覆盖，矛盾。

对积空间应用子基定理（$I=\varnothing$ 或某个 $X_i=\varnothing$ 时结论显然；以下设 $I\ne\varnothing$ 且各 $X_i\ne\varnothing$）。积拓扑的子基是 $\mathcal S=\{\pi_i^{-1}(U_i): i\in I,\ U_i\subset X_i\ \text{开}\}$。设 $\mathcal S'\subset\mathcal S$ 覆盖 $X$；对每个 $i$ 令 $\mathcal U_i=\{U_i\subset X_i\ \text{开}:\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)\in\mathcal S'\}$。若某个 $\mathcal U_{i_0}$ 覆盖 $X_{i_0}$，由 $X_{i_0}$ 紧取有限子覆盖 $U_{i_0,1},\dots,U_{i_0,n}$，对应的 $\pi_{i_0}^{-1}(U_{i_0,k})$ 就是 $\mathcal S'$ 的有限子覆盖。若所有 $\mathcal U_i$ 都不覆盖 $X_i$，则对每个 $i$ 可同时选 $x_i\in X_i\setminus\bigcup\mathcal U_i$；点 $x=(x_i)$ 不属于任何 $\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)\in\mathcal S'$，与 $\mathcal S'$ 覆盖 $X$ 矛盾。因此某个 $\mathcal U_i$ 覆盖 $X_i$，子基定理给出 $X$ 紧。最后一步「对所有 $i$ 同时选 $x_i$」正是选择公理。

边界与推论。箱拓扑下定理失效：$D=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ 是 $\Box_n[0,1]$ 的无限闭离散子空间（每点由 $\prod_n(a_n-1/3,a_n+1/3)$ 孤立），而紧空间不能含无限闭离散子空间，故箱乘积不紧；同样的 $D$ 在积拓扑下就是紧的 Cantor 空间。逻辑上，ZF 中「任意紧空间之积紧」与选择公理等价（Kelley 1950）；限制到紧 Hausdorff 空间则与超滤子引理（BPI）等价，BPI 严格弱于 AC。推论：任意紧 Hausdorff 空间之积仍紧 Hausdorff；$[0,1]^I$、Hilbert 方体 $[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$ 紧；对完全正则 $X$，Stone–Čech 紧化由嵌入 $[0,1]^{C(X,[0,1])}$ 取闭包得到。
en: Tychonoff's theorem: if $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ is a family of compact spaces, then the product $X=\prod_{i\in I}X_i$ is compact in the **product topology**, for an arbitrary index set $I$. The product topology is generated by the subbase of preimages $\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)$ of the projections; equivalently, its basic open sets are products $\prod_i U_i$ with $U_i=X_i$ for all but finitely many $i$. The product topology is essential: with the box topology, which allows genuinely open factors in infinitely many coordinates, the theorem fails.

Finite products via the tube lemma. Let $X,Y$ be compact and let $W\subset X\times Y$ be open with $\{x_0\}\times Y\subset W$. For each $y\in Y$ choose a basic open set $U_y\times V_y\subset W$ containing $(x_0,y)$; the family $\{V_y\}$ covers the compact space $Y$, so finitely many $V_{y_1},\dots,V_{y_n}$ cover $Y$. Put $U=U_{y_1}\cap\cdots\cap U_{y_n}$; then $U\ni x_0$ is open and $U\times Y\subset\bigcup_k U_{y_k}\times V_{y_k}\subset W$, which is the tube lemma. More generally, if a family of open sets $\{W_j\}$ covers the slice $\{x_0\}\times Y$, choose for each $y$ a member $W_{j(y)}$ containing $(x_0,y)$ and a basic open $U_y\times V_y\subset W_{j(y)}$; the same finite-subcover argument gives an open neighbourhood $U$ of $x_0$ such that $U\times Y$ is covered by finitely many $W_j$.

The tube lemma proves $X\times Y$ compact. Let $\{W_j\}$ be an open cover of $X\times Y$. For fixed $x\in X$, the slice $\{x\}\times Y$ is covered; by Step 2 there is an open neighbourhood $U\ni x$ such that $U\times Y$ is covered by finitely many $W_j$. Collect all open sets $U$ with this property into a family $\mathcal U$; it covers the compact space $X$, so finitely many $U_{x_1},\dots,U_{x_m}\in\mathcal U$ cover $X$. Each $U_{x_k}\times Y$ is covered by finitely many $W_j$, and merging these $m$ finite families gives a finite subcover of the original cover. Hence $X\times Y$ is compact. Induction handles any finite product, and only finitely many choices are made, so no choice principle is needed.

Infinite products require Alexander's subbase theorem: if a space has a subbase $\mathcal S$ such that every cover by members of $\mathcal S$ has a finite subcover, then the space is compact. Proof sketch: if some open cover had no finite subcover, Zorn's lemma would give a maximal open cover $\mathcal U$ without a finite subcover. Maximality makes $\mathcal U$ closed under finite intersections: if $U,V\in\mathcal U$ but $U\cap V\notin\mathcal U$, then $\mathcal U\cup\{U\cap V\}$ has a finite subcover, and since $U\cap V\subset U$, replacing $U\cap V$ by $U$ gives a finite subcover of $\mathcal U$, a contradiction. For each $x$, choose $U_x\in\mathcal U$ and subbasic $S_{x,1},\dots,S_{x,m}$ with $x\in\bigcap_j S_{x,j}\subset U_x$. If no $S_{x,j}$ belonged to $\mathcal U$, maximality would give $X=S_{x,j}\cup A_j$ with $A_j$ a finite union of members of $\mathcal U$; hence $$\begin{aligned}X&=\Big(\bigcap_j S_{x,j}\Big)\cup\bigcup_j A_j\\ &\subset U_x\cup\bigcup_j A_j,\end{aligned}$$ and the right-hand side is a finite subcover of $\mathcal U$, a contradiction. Hence the subbasic members of $\mathcal U$ cover $X$; the hypothesis yields a finite subcover, again a finite subcover of $\mathcal U$, a contradiction.

Apply the subbase theorem to the product (the cases $I=\varnothing$ or some $X_i=\varnothing$ are trivial; assume $I\ne\varnothing$ and all $X_i\ne\varnothing$). A subbase for the product topology is $\mathcal S=\{\pi_i^{-1}(U_i): i\in I,\ U_i\subset X_i\ \text{open}\}$. Let $\mathcal S'\subset\mathcal S$ cover $X$, and for each $i$ let $\mathcal U_i=\{U_i\subset X_i\ \text{open}:\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)\in\mathcal S'\}$. If some $\mathcal U_{i_0}$ covers $X_{i_0}$, compactness of $X_{i_0}$ gives finitely many $U_{i_0,1},\dots,U_{i_0,n}$ covering $X_{i_0}$, and the corresponding $\pi_{i_0}^{-1}(U_{i_0,k})$ form a finite subcover from $\mathcal S'$. If no $\mathcal U_i$ covered $X_i$, then for every $i$ we could choose at once a point $x_i\in X_i\setminus\bigcup\mathcal U_i$; the point $x=(x_i)$ would lie in no member of $\mathcal S'$, contradicting that $\mathcal S'$ covers $X$. Hence some $\mathcal U_i$ covers $X_i$, and the subbase theorem gives compactness of $X$. The simultaneous choice of all $x_i$ is exactly where the axiom of choice enters.

Limits and consequences. In the box topology the theorem fails: $D=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ is an infinite closed discrete subspace of $\Box_n[0,1]$ (each point is isolated by $\prod_n(a_n-1/3,a_n+1/3)$), and a compact space cannot contain an infinite closed discrete subspace, so the box product is not compact; the same $D$ in the product topology is the compact Cantor space. Logically, in ZF 「every product of compact spaces is compact」 is equivalent to the axiom of choice (Kelley, 1950); restricted to compact Hausdorff spaces it is equivalent to the ultrafilter lemma (BPI), which is strictly weaker than AC. Consequences: arbitrary products of compact Hausdorff spaces are compact Hausdorff; $[0,1]^I$ and the Hilbert cube $[0,1]^{\mathbb N}$ are compact; for completely regular $X$, the Stone–Čech compactification is obtained by embedding $X$ into $[0,1]^{C(X,[0,1])}$ and taking the closure.

zh: 局部紧：每点 $x$ 有紧邻域，即存在开集 $U\ni x$ 使 $\overline U$ 紧；在 Hausdorff 空间中这等价于存在紧集 $K$ 使 $x\in\operatorname{int}K$。$\mathbb R^n$ 局部紧（闭球是紧邻域）但不紧；紧空间自然局部紧；$\mathbb Q$ 不局部紧——它的紧子集都没有内点（否则在区间内取无理数 $\alpha$，用有理数列逼近它，紧性给出的收敛子列极限既在 $\mathbb Q$ 又等于 $\alpha$，矛盾）。局部紧 Hausdorff 空间完全正则，但不一定正规。

单点紧化（Alexandrov 紧化）构造。设 $X$ 为 Hausdorff 空间。取新点 $\infty\notin X$，令 $X^*=X\cup\{\infty\}$。拓扑规定：$X$ 的开集仍开；$\infty$ 的邻域取 $(X\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$，其中 $K\subset X$ 紧。这些集合构成 $\infty$ 的邻域基：两个这样的邻域之交对应 $K_1\cup K_2$（紧），任意并对应 $\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha$（若非空，是紧集 $K_{\alpha_0}$ 的闭子集，因 $X$ Hausdorff 而紧），与 $X$ 中开集 $U$ 的交为 $U\setminus K$。故拓扑良定义，且 $X$ 在 $X^*$ 中是开集。

$X^*$ 紧。设 $\{V_j\}_{j\in J}$ 是 $X^*$ 的开覆盖。取 $j_0$ 使 $\infty\in V_{j_0}$；因 $V_{j_0}$ 是 $\infty$ 的邻域，存在紧集 $K\subset X$ 使 $(X\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}\subset V_{j_0}$，于是 $X^*\setminus V_{j_0}\subset K$。族 $\{V_j\}_{j\in J}$ 覆盖紧集 $K$，取有限个 $V_{j_1},\dots,V_{j_n}$ 覆盖 $K$；连同 $V_{j_0}$ 得到有限子覆盖。故 $X^*$ 紧。此论证不需要 $X$ 局部紧；若 $X$ 不紧，则每个邻域 $(X\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$ 中 $X\setminus K\ne\varnothing$，故 $X$ 在 $X^*$ 中稠密。

设 $X$ Hausdorff。则 $X^*$ Hausdorff 当且仅当 $X$ 局部紧。若 $X^*$ Hausdorff，取 $x\in X$，把 $x$ 与 $\infty$ 用不交开集 $U,W$ 分开；$W$ 含某个 $(X\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$，故 $U\subset K$，于是 $\overline U\subset K$ 紧（$K$ 在 Hausdorff 的 $X$ 中闭），$X$ 局部紧。反之若 $X$ 局部紧 Hausdorff，$X$ 中两点由 Hausdorff 分离；$x$ 与 $\infty$ 用 $U\ni x$（$\overline U$ 紧）与 $(X\setminus\overline U)\cup\{\infty\}$ 分离。故 $X^*$ Hausdorff。结合第 3 步，不紧的局部紧 Hausdorff 空间 $X$ 得到紧 Hausdorff 紧化 $X^*$。若 $X$ 已紧，则 $K=X$ 使 $\{\infty\}$ 开，$X^*$ 是 $X$ 与孤立点的拓扑和，仍紧 Hausdorff，但 $X$ 不稠密，故它不是 $X$ 的紧化；此时单点紧化通常定义为其自身。

典型例子：$\mathbb R^*\cong S^1$。映射 $$\begin{aligned}\varphi(t)&=\left(\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\right),\\ \varphi(\infty)&=(0,-1),\end{aligned}$$ 取值在 $S^1$ 上，且当 $|t|\to\infty$ 时 $\varphi(t)\to(0,-1)$，故 $\varphi$ 在 $\infty$ 处连续；逆映射在 $S^1\setminus\{(0,-1)\}$ 上为 $(X,Y)\mapsto X/(1+Y)$，连续。于是 $\varphi$ 是连续双射；$X^*$ 紧、$S^1$ Hausdorff，故 $\varphi$ 是同胚。几何上球极投影把 $\mathbb R$ 映成 $S^1$ 去掉南极点，南极点就是 $\infty$；$t\to+\infty$ 与 $t\to-\infty$ 对应同一个点。同理 $\mathbb R^n\cup\{\infty\}\cong S^n$，$\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}=S^2$ 是黎曼球面。

反例与用途。$\mathbb Q$ 不局部紧，故 $\mathbb Q^*$ 紧（第 3 步）但不 Hausdorff（第 4 步）：$\infty$ 的每个邻域 $(\mathbb Q\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$ 中 $K$ 无内点，$\mathbb Q\setminus K$ 稠密，必与任何非空开集相交，无法与 $\mathbb Q$ 的点分离。这说明「单点紧化 Hausdorff」正是局部紧性的判据。紧化的用途是把无穷远处的行为变成一点处的行为：设 $X$ 是不紧的局部紧 Hausdorff 空间，则 $$\begin{aligned}&\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L\\ &\iff f\ \text{延拓为连续}\ F:X^*\to Y,\ F(\infty)=L,\end{aligned}$$ 且 $C_0(X)=\{F|_X:F\in C(X^*),\ F(\infty)=0\}$。对不紧的 $X$，单点紧化还是「最小」紧化：任一紧 Hausdorff 紧化 $Y\supset X$（$X$ 在 $Y$ 中稠密；此时 $X$ 是 $Y$ 的开子集）把 $Y\setminus X$ 压成一点，即得在 $X$ 上恒等的连续满射 $Y\to X^*$。
en: Local compactness: every point $x$ has a compact neighbourhood, i.e. there is an open $U\ni x$ with $\overline U$ compact; in a Hausdorff space this is equivalent to the existence of a compact $K$ with $x\in\operatorname{int}K$. $\mathbb R^n$ is locally compact (closed balls are compact neighbourhoods) but not compact; compact spaces are locally compact; $\mathbb Q$ is not locally compact, since its compact subsets have empty interior (otherwise pick an irrational $\alpha$ in such an interior and rationals approaching it; compactness would give a subsequence converging inside $\mathbb Q$ to $\alpha$, impossible). A locally compact Hausdorff space is completely regular, but need not be normal.

The one-point (Alexandrov) compactification. Assume $X$ is Hausdorff. Adjoin a new point $\infty\notin X$ and set $X^*=X\cup\{\infty\}$. Declare all open sets of $X$ open in $X^*$, and take as neighbourhoods of $\infty$ the sets $(X\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$ with $K\subset X$ compact. These sets form a neighbourhood base at $\infty$: the intersection of two of them corresponds to $K_1\cup K_2$ (compact), the union of a family to $\bigcap_\alpha K_\alpha$ (if nonempty, a closed subset of the compact set $K_{\alpha_0}$, hence compact because $X$ is Hausdorff), and an intersection with an open $U\subset X$ is $U\setminus K$. Thus the topology is well defined, and $X$ is open in $X^*$.

$X^*$ is compact. Let $\{V_j\}_{j\in J}$ be an open cover of $X^*$. Choose $j_0$ with $\infty\in V_{j_0}$; since $V_{j_0}$ is a neighbourhood of $\infty$, it contains some $(X\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$ with $K$ compact, so $X^*\setminus V_{j_0}\subset K$. The family $\{V_j\}_{j\in J}$ covers the compact set $K$, so finitely many $V_{j_1},\dots,V_{j_n}$ cover $K$; together with $V_{j_0}$ they cover $X^*$. Hence $X^*$ is compact. This argument does not need local compactness; if $X$ is noncompact, then $X\setminus K\ne\varnothing$ for every compact $K$, so every neighbourhood of $\infty$ meets $X$ and $X$ is dense in $X^*$.

Assume $X$ Hausdorff. Then $X^*$ is Hausdorff iff $X$ is locally compact. If $X^*$ is Hausdorff, separate $x\in X$ from $\infty$ by disjoint open $U,W$; since $W$ contains some $(X\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$, we get $U\subset K$, so $\overline U\subset K$ is compact ($K$ is closed in the Hausdorff space $X$), and $X$ is locally compact. Conversely, if $X$ is locally compact Hausdorff, two points of $X$ are separated by Hausdorffness, while $x$ and $\infty$ are separated by $U\ni x$ with $\overline U$ compact and by $(X\setminus\overline U)\cup\{\infty\}$. Thus $X^*$ is Hausdorff, and with Step 3 a noncompact locally compact Hausdorff $X$ yields a compact Hausdorff compactification $X^*$. If $X$ is already compact, then $K=X$ makes $\{\infty\}$ open and $X^*$ is the topological sum of $X$ and an isolated point; it is still compact Hausdorff, but $X$ is not dense, so it is not a compactification of $X$. In that case the one-point compactification is usually defined to be $X$ itself.

The standard example: $\mathbb R^*\cong S^1$. The map $$\begin{aligned}\varphi(t)&=\left(\frac{2t}{1+t^2},\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\right),\\ \varphi(\infty)&=(0,-1),\end{aligned}$$ takes values in $S^1$, and $\varphi(t)\to(0,-1)$ as $|t|\to\infty$, so $\varphi$ is continuous at $\infty$. Its inverse on $S^1\setminus\{(0,-1)\}$ is $(X,Y)\mapsto X/(1+Y)$, which is continuous. Hence $\varphi$ is a continuous bijection; since $X^*$ is compact and $S^1$ Hausdorff, it is a homeomorphism. Geometrically, stereographic projection maps $\mathbb R$ onto $S^1$ minus the south pole, and the south pole is $\infty$; both $t\to+\infty$ and $t\to-\infty$ correspond to the same point. Similarly $\mathbb R^n\cup\{\infty\}\cong S^n$, and $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}=S^2$ is the Riemann sphere.

A counterexample and the payoff. $\mathbb Q$ is not locally compact, so $\mathbb Q^*$ is compact by Step 3 but not Hausdorff by Step 4: every neighbourhood of $\infty$ is $(\mathbb Q\setminus K)\cup\{\infty\}$ with $K$ compact, and such a $K$ has empty interior, so $\mathbb Q\setminus K$ is dense and meets every nonempty open set; thus $\infty$ cannot be separated from any point of $\mathbb Q$. This shows that Hausdorffness of the one-point compactification is exactly the local compactness criterion. The use of compactification is to turn behaviour at infinity into behaviour at a point: for a noncompact locally compact Hausdorff $X$, $$\begin{aligned}&\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=L\\ &\iff f\ \text{extends to a continuous}\ F:X^*\to Y\ \text{with}\ F(\infty)=L,\end{aligned}$$ and $C_0(X)=\{F|_X:F\in C(X^*),\ F(\infty)=0\}$. For noncompact $X$, the one-point compactification is also the smallest compactification: any compact Hausdorff compactification $Y\supset X$ (with $X$ dense in $Y$; then $X$ is open in $Y$) yields, by collapsing $Y\setminus X$ to a point, a continuous surjection $Y\to X^*$ that is the identity on $X$.
